Tenth
TENTH
adj. / n.
From Old English teogotha, tenth, the same root that gives tithe. Webster 1828 defines TENTH as the ordinal of ten, and notes that the tenth part is the tithe. In Scripture the word does double service: it names the portion given to God, and it names the remnant God leaves.

Biblical Definition

The tenth is Scripture’s appointed proportion and its picture of a remnant. It appears before the law, in Abraham’s dealing with Melchizedek: he gave him tithes of all (Genesis 14:20), which Hebrews expounds as Abraham gave a tenth part of all (Hebrews 7:2) and then presses into an argument about a priesthood greater than Levi’s — consider how great this man was, unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils (Hebrews 7:4). Under the law it is fixed and unsentimental: concerning the tithe of the herd, or of the flock, even of whatsoever passeth under the rod, the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD (Leviticus 27:32) — the animals filed under the shepherd’s staff and every tenth one counted out, without selection. Even the Levites, who lived on the tithe, tithed it: ye shall offer up an heave offering of it for the LORD, even a tenth part of the tithe (Numbers 18:26). Then Isaiah turns the number toward judgment and hope at once. When the land is emptied, yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak… so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof (Isaiah 6:13). A tenth is what God claims, and a tenth is what God spares.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TENTH as the ordinal of ten, and as a noun, the tenth part — adding that in England the tenths were an ecclesiastical due, and noting the identity of the word with tithe.

expand to see more

TENTH, a. — The ordinal of ten; the first after the ninth.

TENTH, n. — The tenth part; as, he gave a tenth of his substance.

In the older English law, the tenths were the yearly tenth part of the revenue of every ecclesiastical living, paid to the crown.

TITHE is the same word in an older form, from the Saxon teotha, tenth — a fact the English reader loses when the two words are treated as unrelated.

Webster’s ecclesiastical note is a reminder that tithes were long a civil as well as a religious institution in England, which is part of why the word carries such freight in English-speaking churches.

Key Scripture

Genesis 14:20 — "And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all."

Leviticus 27:32 — "And concerning the tithe of the herd, or of the flock, even of whatsoever passeth under the rod, the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD."

Numbers 18:26 — "Thus speak unto the Levites, and say unto them, When ye take of the children of Israel the tithes which I have given you from them for your inheritance, then ye shall offer up an heave offering of it for the LORD, even a tenth part of the tithe."

Hebrews 7:4 — "Now consider how great this man was, unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils."

Isaiah 6:13 — "But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof."

Modern Corruption

The tenth is corrupted in two directions at once: by prosperity teaching that turns it into a deposit on an expected return, and by a careless liberty that treats the New Testament’s silence about a fixed percentage as permission to give nothing in particular.

expand to see more

The prosperity handling of Malachi 3:10 detaches prove me now herewith from a covenant nation under a covenant curse and turns it into a formula for personal return: sow a tenth, reap a hundredfold. The passage is addressed to a people robbing God in a specific ordinance under a specific administration, and the promised blessing is agricultural and national. To make it an investment instrument is to make God a debtor to the giver, which reverses the entire logic of Romans 4:4 — where what is earned is reckoned of debt and not of grace. Giving that expects a yield is not giving; it is a transaction, and the New Testament’s standard is elsewhere: God loveth a cheerful giver, and the Macedonians gave beyond their power out of deep poverty.

The opposite abuse trades on the fact that no fixed percentage is commanded to the church, and quietly concludes that generosity may therefore remain a feeling. But Leviticus 27:32 has the herd passing under the rod with every tenth counted out, unselected and undiscussed, and the whole shape of the law is that giving is decided in advance and by measure rather than in the moment and by mood. Paul keeps that structure exactly when he tells Corinth, upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him. Proportion, regularity, and forethought are all carried over; only the fixed fraction is not commanded. A Christian who gives less thought to his giving than an Israelite gave to his flock has not advanced beyond the law; he has simply stopped counting.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asiri (H6224), tenth, and maaser (H4643), a tithe, from eser (H6235), ten; Greek dekate (G1181), a tenth part.

expand to see more

Hebrew eser (H6235) — ten; the base of the whole family of words.

Hebrew asiri (H6224) — tenth; the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD (Leviticus 27:32).

Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tithe, a tenth part; the standing term for the offering (Numbers 18:26; Malachi 3:10).

Greek dekate (G1181) — a tenth part, a tithe; Hebrews 7:2, 7:4, 7:8, 7:9.

Greek apodekatoo (G586) — to tithe, to pay a tenth; ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin (Matthew 23:23).

Usage

"The tenth shall be holy unto the LORD (Leviticus 27:32) — counted under the rod, not selected."

"Even a tenth part of the tithe (Numbers 18:26) — those who lived on the tithe tithed it."

"Yet in it shall be a tenth… so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof (Isaiah 6:13) — the remnant God keeps."
